attribution.note: Marcus on AI post (co-written, 'our view'), published under Marcus's byline and endorsed. The words are his own description of OpenAI's position, not a quote of someone else.

semantics.note: The normalisation keeps the comparison to public-domain-only training and blanket licensing, and keeps 'apparently' on the payment part. It is a compound observation: a firm part about policy and a hedged part about payment.

contract.note: The contract is fair to his words. It keeps the 'apparently' hedge and does not treat selective licensing as a rebuttal. Because the payment part is hedged and has no definite commitment, the whole compound claim cannot get a firm verdict. The result therefore depends on this reading.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own statement of Jan 8, 2024 defends training on publicly available material as fair use. This is a company disclosure that agrees with the firm policy part, but it says nothing about payment.

AP report of Jan 10, 2024 that OpenAI pays a fee to license AP's archive. This shows some selective paid licensing. It qualifies the payment inference but does not settle the hedged allegation or show a policy of licensing everything.

reviews.rationale: The claim's distinctive allegation, that OpenAI uses copyrighted material without paying, is qualified by 'apparently' and has no definite scope, so under policy it is not scored. The firm part, that OpenAI rejects public-domain-only training or blanket licensing and wants to keep using copyrighted material, agrees with e1. e2 shows some paid licensing. Neither item settles the compound claim, so it is not adjudicable as a whole.
